segments.heading: File header
segments.text:
- The comment still names `bandwidth.c`. This file is the benchmark source before the change of 2026-11-13, and run_kernels.sh built the binary bw_old from it [Ref2].
- The design: each thread owns its buffers. All threads start together. Each thread runs whole passes over its buffer until the minimum time has passed.

`_GNU_SOURCE` makes the Linux-only calls visible, for example `sched_setaffinity` and `CPU_SET` (lines 109 to 112). The headers give the threads (`pthread.h`), the CPU pinning (`sched.h`), `mmap` and `madvise` (`sys/mman.h`), and the clock (`time.h`).

segments.heading: Constants
segments.text:
- `HUGE_BYTES`: 2 MiB (2097152 bytes), the size of one huge page.
- `MAX_CPUS`: the CPU list holds at most 1024 entries.
- `MAX_REPS`: at most 32 timed intervals per kernel.
- `CHECK_BYTES`: 8 MiB. Line 295 divides it by the buffer size. The result, or 1 when the result is 0 (line 297), is the number of passes between two clock reads.
The six kernels of the program. A process runs its selected kernels in this order (loop at line 308). `kernel_name` holds the text that the first column of an output row shows.

segments.heading: Settings and per-thread data
segments.text:
`cfg` holds the settings of the process. The defaults are 1 thread, a minimum time of 0.5 s per interval, 3 intervals per kernel, and a request for 2 MiB pages.
- `cpus`, `ncpus`: the CPU list of the option `--cpus`.
- `bytes`: the buffer size of each thread.
- `run[k]`: 1 when kernel k is selected.
- `per_thread`: 1 with the option `--per-thread`. The comment in line 37 is out of date. The code prints one line per thread and repetition, with the rate of that repetition (lines 452 to 456).

- `struct result`: the bytes that one thread moved in one timed interval, and the time that the same thread measured for it.
- `struct thread`: one entry per thread. It holds the thread index, the CPU, the buffers `a` and `b`, and one result per kernel and interval.

`bar` is a barrier. A thread that calls `pthread_barrier_wait(&bar)` waits until all worker threads and the main thread have called it. Then all of them continue together. Line 402 sets how many threads must arrive.

segments.heading: Function `now_s`: read the clock
segments.text: Reads `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` (the Linux clock that only moves forward) and returns it in seconds as a `double`. Every time value of the program comes from this function.

segments.heading: Function `parse_bytes`: read a size such as `256M`
segments.text: Reads a number and an optional suffix: `k` means 2^10, `m` means 2^20, `g` means 2^30 (upper case too). `256M` gives 268435456 bytes (256 MiB). A text that is not a positive size ends the program with exit status 2.

segments.heading: Function `parse_cpus`: read the CPU list
segments.text:
- Cuts the list at each comma.
- Each piece is one number, a range `lo-hi`, or a range with a step `lo-hi:step`.
- Every CPU number is appended to `cfg.cpus` in the order of the list.
- `0-119` gives the 120 entries 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 119.
- A bad piece ends the program with exit status 2.

segments.heading: Function `pin_cpu`: pin the calling thread to one CPU
segments.text: Builds a CPU set that holds one CPU and passes it to `sched_setaffinity`. The first argument 0 means the calling thread, so only this thread is pinned. After the call Linux runs the thread only on that CPU. If the call fails, the program ends with exit status 2.

segments.heading: Function `alloc_buf`: reserve one buffer on a 2 MiB boundary
segments.text:
- `len`: the size rounded up to a multiple of 2 MiB. 256 MiB stays 256 MiB.
- `mmap` reserves `len` plus 2 MiB of private memory that belongs to no file.
- `mmap` reserves addresses only. Linux assigns the physical memory when a page is first written (line 302).
- If `mmap` fails, the program ends with exit status 2.

- `p`: the first address in the reserved range that is a multiple of 2 MiB. The buffer starts there.
- `madvise` with `MADV_HUGEPAGE` asks Linux to use 2 MiB pages for the buffer. With the option `--no-thp` it passes `MADV_NOHUGEPAGE`, which forbids them.
- ra.sh does not pass `--no-thp`, so the whole-chip test asks for 2 MiB pages [Ref3].
- A failed `madvise` only prints a message. The program never checks whether the buffer in fact lies on 2 MiB pages.
- The program never releases the buffer.

segments.heading: Function `k_read`: the OLD read kernel
segments.text:
- The comment gives the intent of the 16 sums. An add to one sum does not wait for an add to another sum. So the loads, not the adds, are meant to set the speed of the loop. This file holds no measurement of that.
- The NEON sentence names 8 vector chains. This count holds for bw_old: its machine code has 8 vector registers for the sums, each with two 64-bit sums [Ref1].
- The AVX-512 sentence is about x86 processors. It does not apply to CRB.

`noinline` forbids the compiler to merge the kernel into its caller. So the binary holds `k_read` as a function of its own, and run_kernels.sh printed its machine code by name [Ref1]. `a` is the buffer of the thread. `n` is the number of 8-byte elements in the buffer (line 291).
16 running sums of 64 bits each, all 0 at the start. In bw_old the compiler keeps them in the 8 vector registers `v24` to `v31` during the loop. Each register holds two of the sums [Ref1].

The outer loop. One loop pass handles 16 elements, which is 128 B. A buffer of 256 MiB needs 2097152 loop passes. `main` accepts only buffer sizes that are a multiple of 256 B (line 392), so the loop ends exactly at the end of the buffer.

The inner loop of the source: 16 steps per outer loop pass, one step per sum. The machine code of bw_old has no inner loop. gcc turned its 16 loads and 16 adds into vector instructions [Ref1]. One loop pass of the machine code is one pass of the outer loop (128 B).

Source: load one 8-byte element and add it to its own sum. Every loaded value is used. One loop pass of the machine code of bw_old has 16 instructions [Ref1]:
- 4 `ldp q` loads. Each one loads two 16-byte vector registers, so each one reads 32 B.
- 8 vector `add` instructions. Each one adds one loaded register (two 64-bit values) to one of the 8 sum registers.
- 2 scalar `add` instructions: the loop counter plus 1, and the buffer pointer plus 128 B.
- 1 `cmp` and 1 conditional branch back to the first load.
- Per 256 B this is 8 `ldp q` loads and 16 vector adds, 32 instructions in total. The new read kernel of bw_new has the same 8 `ldp q` loads per 256 B and no vector add, 11 instructions in total [Ref1].

After the loop: add the 16 sums to one value and return it. This runs once per call, so once per pass over the buffer. In bw_old the code outside the loop also sets the sums to 0 and stores them to the stack. It also holds a stack check that is not in the source (a call of `__stack_chk_fail`) [Ref1].

segments.heading: Function `k_write`: C write kernel, also used for the first touch
segments.text: Stores the value `v` into each of the `n` elements. The worker also calls it once per buffer for the first touch (lines 302 and 305). In bw_old gcc made an SVE loop from it, with one `st1d` vector store per loop pass [Ref1]. The objdump text does not show the vector length.

segments.heading: Function `k_copy`: C copy kernel
segments.text: Copies `n` elements from `s` to `d`. `restrict` tells the compiler that the two buffers do not overlap. In bw_old gcc made an SVE loop from it, with one `ld1d` vector load and one `st1d` vector store per loop pass [Ref1].

segments.heading: The asm kernels (64-bit Arm only)
segments.text:
- These three kernels are assembly text inside a C function. The compiler copies the loop. It only puts a register in the place of each name such as `%[p]` [Ref1]. It cannot add, reorder or remove an instruction.
- Each loop pass handles 256 B of the buffer: with 8 `ldp q` loads, with 8 `stp q` stores, or with both in `k_asmcopy`.
- The Arm calling rules say that a function must keep the lower halves (`d8` to `d15`) of the registers `v8` to `v15` for its caller. So the compiler saves and restores them once per call, outside the loop. The objdump text of `k_asmread` and `k_asmcopy` shows this [Ref1].
- `HAVE_ASM_KERNELS` is 1 when the three kernels exist.

segments.heading: Function `k_asmread`: hand-written load-only loop
segments.text: `p` starts at the first element of the buffer. `end` is the address directly after the last element. The function returns nothing.

One loop pass:
- 8 `ldp q` loads read 256 B into the registers `q0` to `q15`. Each load reads 32 B.
- `add` moves the pointer forward by 256 B.
- `cmp` and `b.lo` repeat the loop while the pointer is below `end`.
- The loaded values are never used. The next loop pass overwrites them.
- This is 11 instructions per 256 B. The objdump text of bw_old shows the same 11 instructions [Ref1].

These three lists tell the compiler what the assembly text uses. `p` is read and changed in a register. `end` is read in a register. The last list names what the text changes or accesses without an operand: the registers `v0` to `v15`, memory, and the condition flags (`cc`).

segments.heading: Function `k_asmwrite`: hand-written store-only loop
segments.text: `dup` fills the register `v0` with two copies of the 64-bit value `v`, once before the loop. Each loop pass stores 256 B with 8 `stp q0, q0` instructions of 32 B each. Then `add` moves the pointer forward by 256 B, and the loop repeats while the pointer is below `end`.

segments.heading: Function `k_asmcopy`: hand-written copy loop
segments.text: Each loop pass first loads 256 B from `s` with 8 `ldp q` instructions. It then stores the same 16 registers to `d` with 8 `stp q` instructions. Both pointers move forward by 256 B, and the loop repeats while the source pointer is below `end`.
On a processor that is not 64-bit Arm the three asm kernels are not compiled. `HAVE_ASM_KERNELS` is then 0, and `main` refuses to run them (line 394).

segments.heading: Function `pass`: one pass of kernel `k` over the buffer
segments.text:
Runs the kernel `k` once over the whole buffer of thread `t`. It returns the number of bytes that the caller counts for this pass.
- `n`: the number of 8-byte elements.
- `v`: the value for the write kernels.
- `sink`: a pointer to a variable on the stack of the calling thread (line 292).

Kernel `read`: call `k_read`, the old read kernel, on buffer `a`, and store the returned sum to `*sink`.
- `sink` is `volatile`, so the compiler must do this store. It therefore cannot remove the sum, the adds or the loads.
- This is one 8-byte store per pass over the buffer.
- The pass counts `cfg.bytes`, the buffer size. It is 268435456 bytes in the whole-chip test.
Kernel `write`: fill buffer `a` with the value `v`. The pass counts the buffer size once.
Kernel `copy`: copy buffer `a` to buffer `b`. The pass counts the buffer size twice: the bytes read plus the bytes written.
Kernel `asmread` (compiled on 64-bit Arm only): call `k_asmread` on buffer `a`. `k_asmread` returns no value, so nothing is stored to `sink`. The pass counts the buffer size once.
Kernel `asmwrite`: the same as `write`, with the hand-written loop.
Kernel `asmcopy`: the same as `copy`, with the hand-written loop. It also counts the buffer size twice.
Any other value counts 0 bytes. This line is reached only for an asm kernel in a build without the asm kernels. `main` stops such a run before it creates the threads (line 394).

segments.heading: Function `worker`: one benchmark thread
segments.text: Each thread that `main` creates (line 409) runs this function once. `t` is the entry of this thread in the thread table.
`n`: the number of 8-byte elements in the buffer. It is 33554432 for a buffer of 256 MiB.
`sink`: the variable that receives the sum of `k_read` (line 264). It lies on the stack of this thread. So the 120 threads do not store to one shared cache line.
`v`: the value that the write kernels store. It is computed from the process id and the thread index, so the compiler does not know it. The read kernels do not use it.

`passes_per_check`: the number of passes between two clock reads. It is 8 MiB divided by the buffer size, and at least 1. For a buffer of 256 MiB the division gives 0, so the value is 1. The thread then reads the clock after every pass.
When a CPU list was given, the thread pins itself to its CPU. In the whole-chip test thread i runs on CPU i (line 408). The thread does this before it reserves its buffer.

Reserve buffer `a` and write `v` into every element with `k_write`. This write is the first touch: Linux assigns the physical memory of the buffer now, while the thread already runs on its CPU. It is not timed.
Only when `copy` or `asmcopy` is selected: reserve and write a second buffer `b`. In the whole-chip test a process of the read kernel has one buffer of 256 MiB per thread.

Loop over the six kernels in the order of the `enum` (line 25). A kernel that is not selected is skipped. ra.sh selects one kernel per process. So in the whole-chip test no kernel is timed after another kernel in the same process [Ref3].
For each repetition (3 in the whole-chip test): first run one pass that is not timed (warm-up).

Wait at the barrier until all 120 workers and the main thread have arrived. A thread that arrives early waits here and reads no memory. The barrier then releases all threads at the same time. This is the common start of the timed interval.

`t0`: the clock read directly after the barrier. It is the start of the timed interval of this thread. Each thread has its own `t0`. `bytes` counts the bytes of this interval, and `p` counts its passes.

The timed work. The inner `for` runs `passes_per_check` passes (1 in the whole-chip test) and adds the byte count of each pass to `bytes`. For kernel `read` each pass is one call of `k_read` over the whole buffer. `v + p` gives the write kernels a new value in every pass.

`t1`: the clock read after the passes. The loop repeats while less than `cfg.min_s` has passed since `t0` (0.5 s in the whole-chip test).
- A thread never stops inside a pass. In the whole-chip test its interval ends at the first end of a pass that lies 0.5 s or more after `t0`.
- The threads therefore stop at different times.

Store the result of this thread for this kernel and repetition: the bytes counted and the time `t1 - t0`. The time covers the passes and the clock reads between them. It does not cover the warm-up pass or the waits at the barrier.

Wait at the barrier until all workers have finished the interval and the main thread has arrived. A thread that stopped early waits here and reads no memory while the other threads finish their last pass.

End of the repetition loop and of the kernel loop. The next repetition starts with its warm-up pass directly after the barrier. The code has no sleep there. The thread ends after the last repetition of the last selected kernel.

segments.heading: Function `usage`: print the options and stop
segments.text: Prints the list of options to the error output and ends the program with exit status 2.

segments.heading: Function `main`: arguments, threads, rates
segments.text: Defaults before the arguments are read: a buffer of 1 MiB per thread, and the three C kernels `read`, `write` and `copy` selected.

Loop over the arguments. `more` is true when one more argument follows, which an option with a value needs.
- `--no-thp` forbids 2 MiB pages (line 130).
- `--per-thread` adds one output line per thread and repetition (line 449).
- ra.sh passes neither of the two [Ref3].

Options with a value. The values of the whole-chip test come from ra.sh [Ref3].
- `--threads`: the number of threads. ra.sh passes 120.
- `--cpus`: the CPU list, read by `parse_cpus`. ra.sh passes `0-119`.
- `--bytes`: the buffer size of each thread, read by `parse_bytes`. ra.sh passes `256M` (256 MiB).
- `--min-ms`: the minimum time of an interval, changed from ms to seconds. ra.sh passes 500, which gives 0.5 s.
- `--reps`: the number of timed intervals per kernel. ra.sh passes 3.

- `--kernel`: first clear every selection, then select the named kernel.
- `all` selects the three C kernels, and `asmall` selects the three asm kernels.
- Any other name prints the option list and stops.
- ra.sh passes one kernel name per process. One call of ra.sh starts bw_old with each of the six names twice, once per round [Ref3].
An unknown argument, or an option without its value, prints the option list and stops.

Checks of the arguments. A failed check prints the option list and ends the program with exit status 2.
- `--threads` is accepted only together with `--cpus`.
- The thread count must be 1 or more. The repetitions must be 1 to 32.
- The buffer size must be a multiple of 256 B. Every kernel then ends exactly at the end of the buffer: `k_read` moves in steps of 128 B, the asm kernels in steps of 256 B.

An asm kernel on a processor that is not 64-bit Arm ends the program with exit status 2. More threads than CPUs in the list only gives a warning. The list is then used again from its start (line 408). The whole-chip test has 120 threads on 120 CPUs.

Allocate the thread table, filled with zeros. Create the barrier for `cfg.threads + 1` threads: the workers plus the main thread. In the whole-chip test this is 121. A failure ends the program with exit status 2.

Create the threads.
- Thread `i` gets the index `i` and the CPU `cfg.cpus[i % cfg.ncpus]`. With the list `0-119` and 120 threads, thread i gets CPU i.
- Each thread starts `worker` immediately: it pins itself, reserves and writes its buffer, runs the first warm-up pass and then waits at the barrier.
- If a thread cannot be created, the program ends with exit status 2.
Print two header lines to the standard output. The first starts with `#` and gives the rate formula and the settings of the process. The second holds the 10 column names of the interval rows.

segments.heading: Rate computation: one row per timed interval
segments.text: Loop over the kernels in the same order as the workers (line 308), with the same skip rule. `best` will hold the highest total rate of the repetitions of this kernel.

One repetition, as the main thread sees it:
- First wait: the barrier opens when the main thread and all workers have arrived. The workers then start their timed interval (line 314).
- Second wait: it returns when every worker has finished its interval (line 323).
- The main thread does no work during the interval. The program does not pin the main thread.
Start values for one row: `total` (bytes of all threads), `max_el` (longest thread time), and `mn`, `mx`, `sum` (lowest, highest and sum of the thread rates).
For each thread: `g` is the rate of this thread in GB/s. It is the bytes of the thread, divided by the time of the same thread, divided by 1e9.
Add the bytes of the thread to `total`. Keep the longest thread time in `max_el`.
Keep the lowest and the highest thread rate. Add the thread rate to `sum` for the mean.

- `agg`: the total rate of the interval in GB/s. It is the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest thread time, divided by 1e9.
- The output column is `aggregate_GBps`.
- A thread with a shorter time adds no bytes after its own stop. So `agg` is never above the sum of the thread rates.
Keep the highest `agg` of the repetitions in `best`.

Print one interval row. Its columns are:
- the kernel name, the thread count, the buffer size per thread in bytes, the repetition number (counted from 0)
- `total_bytes`: `total`
- `elapsed_s`: `max_el`, with 4 decimals
- `aggregate_GBps`: `agg`, with 2 decimals
- the lowest, the highest and the mean thread rate in GB/s, with 2 decimals. The mean is `sum / cfg.threads`.

After the last repetition: print the `best` row. Its column `aggregate_GBps` holds the highest `agg` of the repetitions. The columns `total_bytes` and `elapsed_s` and the three thread-rate columns are empty. The analysis scripts stat_k120.py and facts_data.py do not use this row [Ref4].
Only with `--per-thread`: print one more line per thread and repetition. ra.sh does not pass this option, and the files of the whole-chip test hold no such line [Ref3] [Ref5].

Each line holds the word `thread`, the thread index, the CPU, the kernel, the repetition and the thread rate in GB/s. The rate is the bytes of the thread, divided by the time of the same thread, divided by 1e9.
`fflush` writes the buffered rows of this kernel to the output now.
Wait until every worker thread has ended. Then end the process with exit status 0.
